plan.question: How did a border clash between regional rivals pull global superpowers into the Persian Gulf?

chapters.title: A Chokepoint on Fire
beats: A grinding war between two Middle Eastern neighbors spills into the vital waterways of the Persian Gulf, threatening the flow of crude oil feeding world industries.
Both governments unleash naval raids and air strikes directly against international commercial merchant ships and foreign tankers.
As hundreds of commercial vessels sustain damage and sea lanes turn hazardous, an outside superpower sails directly into the contested waters to shield foreign commerce.

chapters.title: The Rival Rulers
beats: The Persian Gulf is the vital marine corridor through which regional crude leaves for world markets, making its narrow waterways and island terminals strategic lifelines for both Iraq and Iran.

In Baghdad, Iraq, Saddam Hussein consolidates supreme authority as president, determined to dominate regional waterways, control navigation through the Shatt al-Arab river, and assert his nation's primacy.

Opposing him across the border is Ruhollah Khomeini, the revolutionary cleric who establishes the Islamic Republic of Iran after decades of exile, determined to export revolutionary clerical rule and dismantle secular regimes.
Watching from Washington, Ronald Reagan seeks to preserve international navigation, protect allied Gulf oil exporters, and counter any expansion of hostile revolutionary power in vital sea lanes.

chapters.title: From River to Open Sea
beats: In 1975, Iraq and Iran sign the Algiers Agreement settling boundary disputes along the Shatt al-Arab river, but friction deepens after the 1979 revolution brings Ruhollah Khomeini to power.
Saddam Hussein assumes the Iraqi presidency in July 1979, and by September 1980 launches an invasion of Iran across the disputed frontier.
The ground assault stalls by December 1980, prompting UN Secretary General Kurt Waldheim to appeal for peaceful shipping security as fighting threatens maritime commerce.
In May 1981, Iraq inaugurates the Tanker War by proclaiming it will attack vessels traveling to or from northern Iranian ports.
By June 1982, the Iranian military recaptures its lost territory and expels Iraqi ground units back to pre-war borders, prompting Iraq to look toward maritime targets.
chapters.hook: Unable to break the Iranian ground defenses, Baghdad seeks to choke Tehran's economy at sea.

chapters.title: Striking the Terminals
beats: In 1984, Saddam Hussein broadens maritime operations by ordering strikes against the vital Iranian oil terminal and loaded tankers at Kharg Island.
Ruhollah Khomeini and Iranian commanders respond by striking back against merchant traffic sailing toward Arab ports friendly to Baghdad.
Over the campaign, Iraq executes 283 attacks against merchant vessels, while Iranian forces conduct 168 strikes on commercial shipping.
Iran imposes an exclusion zone stretching 40 miles from its coast, targeting neutral vessels while cargo damage mounts past 30 million tons.
Neutral merchant seamen suffer heavy casualties across the shipping channels, with well over 100 sailors killed as missiles and mines ravage commercial traffic.

chapters.title: The Reflagging Decision
beats: In January 1987, the government of Kuwait proposes to reflag its commercial tankers under the American flag to secure armed US Navy protection.
Inside the White House, President Ronald Reagan evaluates the request to safeguard maritime commerce and prevent rival influence over Gulf shipping.
On 7 March 1987, Ronald Reagan formally agrees to reflag Kuwaiti tankers, committing the United States military directly into the contested waters of the Persian Gulf.

chapters.title: Operation Earnest Will and the Aftermath
beats: Tensions explode on 17 May 1987 when an Iraqi aircraft strikes the USS Stark in the Persian Gulf, killing 37 US sailors.
On 20 July 1987, the United Nations Security Council unanimously adopts Resolution 598 demanding an immediate ceasefire.
Four days later, on 24 July 1987, US forces launch Operation Earnest Will to escort reflagged Kuwaiti merchant vessels through the Gulf.
Following Iranian strikes and naval clashes, American warships confront Iranian forces while escorting merchant tankers past minefields and missile batteries.
By mid-1988, Iraqi counter-offensives stall into a stalemate along the Iran–Iraq border, leading to a general ceasefire that brings Operation Earnest Will to a close on 26 September 1988.
The overall Iran–Iraq War claims around 500,000 deaths and leaves Iraq burdened with $561 billion in economic losses.
In 1990, Saddam Hussein accuses Kuwait of slant-drilling Iraqi oil fields and invades the emirate, sparking the Gulf War.
In 2003, the United States and allied forces invade Iraq, leading to the overthrow and capture of Saddam Hussein, who is convicted of crimes against humanity and executed on 30 December 2006.

script.title: Tankers Are Burning in Hormuz Again. In 1987 It Pulled America Into War
script.description: This week Iran's Revolutionary Guard reported three tankers on fire in the Strait of Hormuz. Almost forty years ago, the same waters saw the Tanker War: Iraq and Iran attacked hundreds of merchant ships, Kuwait put its tankers under the American flag, and the US Navy ended up fighting Iran at sea, then shot down Iran Air Flight 655.
script.comment_question: Which moment made the war at sea impossible to stop: the Stark, the Bridgeton mine, or Praying Mantis?
